course_details.Meeting Info: Kresge 3438 Philosophy Sem. Rm: Tues, Thurs 11:00AM - 12:20PM
course_details.Overview of class: In the Republic, Plato uses the "Kallipolis"—the beautiful city—as a hypothetical arrangement to explore questions of justice, the soul, governance, the family, education, art, and more. This course will explore such questions as: What is a city? How should a city be governed? What does it mean to be a "city person"? How does living in a city shape our identities, habits, attitudes, and virtues/vices? How does the city influence our relationship to bodies—our own, and those of others? What is the relationship between the city and autonomy, creativity, democracy, and diversity? We will explore these questions by progressing through ways the city was conceived within the history of philosophy (eg, Plato) move into more modern conceptions (eg, Hannah Arendt) and eventually engage with philosophically-oriented analyses of current issues such as gentrification, tourism, sanctuary cities, and sustainability. Students will have occasion to discuss these readings alongside their experiences living in different kinds of political and spatial arrangements. Throughout the course, we will focus on how to become effective writers by transitioning from oral discussions and shorter, informal reflections into more formal, sophisticated written work.

course_details.Topic: Being and Becoming: An Introduction to Western Met
course_details.Meeting Info: Kresge 3438 Philosophy Sem. Rm: Tues, Thurs 12:30PM - 1:50PM
course_details.Overview of class:
Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that asks some of the most fundamental questions about reality and existence. What does it mean for something to exist? What is reality as a whole? How can something remain the same while changing over time? Is the world we experience real, or could it be an illusion? Why does anything exist at all rather than nothing?
Many of these questions lead to a central debate in metaphysics: the relationship between Being and Becoming and which counts as ‘true reality.' Being has often been thought as what is real, lasting, or unchanging, while Becoming has been thought of as its opposite, referring to the world of change, growth, and passing away. Throughout the history of Western philosophy, thinkers have disagreed about how we should understand this relationship. Some have argued that what is truly real must be permanent and unchanging, such as an eternal idea, God, or an underlying essence. From this perspective, the changing world we experience may seem less real or less fundamental. Other philosophers have challenged this view, arguing that change is not something separate from reality but is part of what reality itself is.
In this course we will study this age-old debate by considering some of its central figures and their various arguments. Readings will include selections from Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Descartes, Nietzsche, and Heidegger. Due to the immensity of this historical debate, we can only survey some of the key turns that have profoundly shaped the tradition.Throughout the course, we will also ask a broader question: How might our understanding of reality shape the way we live? In other words, what difference would it make to our lives if we accepted one philosopher's account of what is truly real over another's?
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Students will develop an overview understanding of one of the deepest questions the history of western philosophy has grappled with, gaining an appreciation for its complexities and implications for how we lead our lives.

Students will also learn about various key western philosophical thinkers and their transformative contributions to western philosophy.

Students will develop reading comprehension and oral presentation skills through course assignments.

Students will also develop their ability to think through difficult, often unanswerable, questions and learn to pose further questions as we go along the course. They will find that open questions are very productive, even if they remain unsolved.

course_details.Overview of class: In this course, we will consider the origins of Western philosophy, from the Presocratics to some of the main traditions of the Hellenistic period, Stoicism and skepticism. We will occasionally contrast these Greek and Roman views with those of other traditions in world philosophy. Readings will include Heraclitus, Parmenides, Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, and Sextus Empiricus.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
"This course aims to meet the Weinberg learning objectives for both Historical Studies and Ethical and Evaluative Thinking as follows:

Historical Studies:
• Acquire knowledge of historical phenomena and become familiar with relevant primary sources: we will consider the central philosophical developments in the Ancient Greek and Roman world, with much of our attention given to reading primary sources.
• Develop skills of historical analysis, including the means to evaluate sources: we will read these philosophical texts against the context of their intellectual and political backdrop, focusing on both their argumentative structure and their cultural impact.
• Appreciate the impact of historical developments and acquire historical perspective on the present: we will trace the development of several schools of thought as they interact with each other, while also considering some points of comparison with intellectual traditions outside of Europe.
• Express the results of historical investigation effectively and persuasively and engage in debate with other narrators and interpreters of history, both past and present: we will hone the critical reading and writing skills needed to present the central points of view, along with their argumentative underpinnings, and we will understand how later philosophers (both in and outside of these traditions) have understood the central texts.

Ethical and Evaluative Thinking:
• Attain the conceptual tools needed to recognize and understand prescriptive issues, questions and claims, and to distinguish them from descriptive issues, questions, and claims: we will examine how evaluative claims (e.g., about the nature of the good) were often used to underpin descriptive claims about the nature of the universe and the human mind.
• Identify the values presupposed by an outlook or discourse: we will examine some of the central developments in ancient philosophy, as distinctive argument forms and theories take shape.
• Recognize the complexity of many ethical issues and consider a variety of alternative resolutions and the reasons for holding them: we will look at a variety of ethical and evaluative issues (e.g., the nature of virtue), as well as their impact on broader philosophical systems.
• Appreciate the insights available in one or more intellectual or cultural traditions: we will look at the intersections and divergences between various intellectual and cultural traditions, including pro- and anti-democratic thinkers, new forms of metaphysical theorizing, and inquiry into the nature and extent of human knowledge; we will also look at how these developments appear from the point of view of some non-European philosophers.
• Reflect upon one's own answers to evaluative questions, the presuppositions informing them, and the reasons supporting them: we will develop our own interpretations of, and responses to, the ancient philosophers we read, and we will develop our own views about the issues they consider, while uncovering the ways in which our presuppositions may differ from theirs.
• Engage in respectful, rigorous, and constructive dialogue concerning evaluative issues and communicate thoughtfully and clearly about them: we will engage in a variety of individual and group activities that will foster a capacity for critical, charitable discussion, both verbally and in writing."

course_details.Overview of class: This course is about ways to change and vary the logics presented in PHIL 150 (Propositional logic, and first-order logic), and how these can and have been used to address philosophical questions. We'll examine questions of ontology--what there is--and what logic has to do with that question. We'll ask about the nature of the identity relation, and so concern ourselves with what sorts of notions are logical. We'll ask after the relation between truth and meaning, and whether classical logic (as was presented in PHIL 150) is accurate to a sophisticated understanding of these topics. We'll also spend a good amount of time on normal modal logics, which can be interpreted as addressing questions of possibility and necessity--and which circle back to questions of ontology. We will also address how to understand counterfactual conditionals, such as "If Harris had been elected, Parton wouldn't have died yet." Additional topics as time allows.

course_name: Introduction to Philosophy of the Natural Sciences

course_info.course_name: Introduction to Philosophy of the Natural Sciences

course_details.Overview of class: The course will introduce students to metaphysical and epistemological issues raised by modern natural science. We will be guided by nested "what does it take"-questions. For example: What does it take for natural science to be -in societies with a scientific culture—the legitimate authority on matters of fact about nature? What does it take for a system of assertions to count as a good scientific theory? What does it take for a scientific theory to be testable by evidence like observational and experimental data (and: what does it take for certain series of experiences to count as data, observations, experimental results?)? What does it take for a given theory to be better supported by the available evidence than its competitors? What does it take for a given theory to explain the known phenomena in an area of knowledge? What does it take for an explanatory scientific theory to be credited with reference to underlying structures of reality? We will begin with a brief overview of the scientific revolution of the 16th and 17 th century, and then turn to contemporary discussions on the problem of induction, the problem of the underdetermination of theory choice by the available data, the problem of rationality, the problem of realism. This will include reflecting on reasons philosophers of science have established against some common preconceptions about what it takes to be entitled to scientific objectivity, such as that science provides ‘proof', or that there is one simple, context-free ‘scientific method', or that scientific objectivity is free of considerations of values or informed judgment. Many contemporary doubt-manufacturers selectively use parts of such reasons to suggest the skeptical attitude that science produces just one among many optional beliefs about reality, and that others (like religion, or what serves the oil industry) are equally valid. Against this, we will see that the reasons against proof as the standard (and in favor of evidential support and fallibility) in fact don't weaken but instead strengthen the justifications of why we ought to trust scientifically formed belief where it and its institutional and social conditions are available more than any other (purported) sources of information on nature.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Having worked through the materials offered, students will... -be competent in the major paradigms and revolutions behind contemporary natural science -be able to identify, discuss and appreciate foundations of advanced scientific theories that use vocabulary referring to entities not observable by the human perceptual equipment -be able to conduct a formally correct argument articulating methodological and/or ontological and/or evaluative aspects of scientific work -Have gained an appreciation of the deep reach of human factors in scientific practice (like background understandings, relevance constraints, comparative judgments) of even the natural sciences, and thereby have acquired a sophisticated concept of scientific objectivity.

course_details.Overview of class:
In this class we will investigate several philosophical questions that arise as we think about knowledge. We will consider questions concerning the values that arise in connection with knowledge and other products of inquiry, we will help students recognize and reflect on evaluative questions that arise when we assess claims to knowledge, we will become aware of the standards we bring to bear in such assessments, and we will appreciate how these standards may be misused, abused, or exploited under certain social conditions.

The sorts of question we will address include: Are we free to believe as we like? And even if we are, under what conditions, if any, should we deviate from what the evidence supports? To what extent should we think for ourselves, and when if at all should we rely on experts? What (if anything) is wrong with information bubbles? What is the responsible way to consume news? How do we determine when our beliefs are rational, and what can be done when we detect irrationality (in ourselves or others)? What should we do when we disagree? What is the nature of trust (and when should we trust)?
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• To understand the difference between descriptions and evaluations, and to acquire the tools needed to assess both types of claim
• To identify the values that are presupposed by each of the perspectives we consider
• To recognize the complexity of ethical decision-making (and the reasons that support such decisions)
• To appreciate the insights present in various intellectual or cultural traditions
• To reflect competently on one's own answers to evaluative questions, the presuppositions informing one's answers, and the reasons supporting them
• To engage in respectful, rigorous, and constructive discussion when disagreeing about values, and to communicate one's claims thoughtfully and clearly

course_details.Overview of class: In this course, we will consider what makes for a good life from birth to death. We will ask questions like these : is coming into existence bad for you? Is being born with a disability a harm? Is being a child good for you? How much freedom should teenagers be afforded? How can college change you for better or worse? What do parents owe their children? Is living a good life incompatible with living a moral life? What would it mean for your life to go well anyway? What is the "midlife crisis" and how could we navigate it? How can we age thoughtfully and what do we owe our elders? Is death bad? Would it be desirable to live forever? Via considering these questions, we will also focus on becoming clearer and more persuasive writers.

course_details.Overview of class: This course provides a thorough reading of the conception of empirical knowledge laid out in the first part of Kant\'s "Critique of Pure Reason" (the Analytic). The seminar will also relate Kant\'s arguments to issues in more recent philosophical debates. E.g.: Kant qualified his philosophy as "transcendental idealism and empirical realism". According to Kant, it evades the choice between saying that we must have an unconceptualized access to reality in order to have factual knowledge (so that it is hard to say how we as concept-using knowers can know reality at all) on the one hand, and saying that the reality our factual knowledge represents is determined by our concepts (so that it is hard to say in what way reality is a mind-independent constraint on belief). Kant suggests that this is a non-issue if there is only one universal set of concepts constitutive of all (genuinely fact-enabling) human experience. But the course of scientific progress since reveals this as a big (and unfulfilled) IF: in light of the diversity of experience and of the sciences, it is not easy to insist that there is only one set of forms of all possible objects of experience, one set of categories to form judgments, one set of principles to form natural laws. But the impasse confronted in Kant\'s epistemological analysis persists --for each of the variegated forms. Can Kant\'s conception of experience and empirical knowledge still help us understand how we can claim to know mind-independent reality? Another example: Much of contemporary philosophy of mind centers on the question of the relation between mind and reality. Kant criticized all such attempts at founding factual knowledge on self-knowledge (which lead into "paralogisms") or knowledge of unconceptualised reality in itself (which lead to "antinomies"). His arguments compel realizing that both (reality as such and a directly present foundational \'inner\' self) can\'t be objects of knowledge at all (=are non-objects). Does this dissolve the problems of mind and reality or rather make them cognitively insolvable?
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students will become familiar with one of the classic texts of the Western philosophical tradition. They will acquire conceptual, theoretical, epistemological abilities to analyze complex dependencies between basic commonsense assumptions about factual knowledge and their internal tensions. In doing so, the students\' analytic, critical, but also their literary and imaginative capacities will be relied on but also expanded into previously uncharted terrain. Finally, it is hoped that students learn that and how insights in a historical text of a given tradition can matter to extremely contemporary issues (e.g. the distinction between real news and constructed pseudo-facts).

course_details.Overview of class:
Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Ramsey

Modern logic begins with Gottlob Frege, a mathematician whose striking insights and methods also produced a compelling approach to philosophy. This course will explore, in the writings of Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, and Ramsey, a question that arises from Frege's approach: to what extent does having a logic, or a philosophy of logic, constitute having the rest of philosophy--for examples: an epistemology, a metaphysics, even an ethics? As time allows we'll look at the nearby work of G.E. Moore and Susan Stebbing.

A course in logic (such as PHIL 150 or PHIL 250) may be helpful for this course, but is not required.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
To comprehend a selection of the major works of, and interpretive approaches to, Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, and Ramsey.

To articulate in written and verbal form the main issues that concerned these writers, and how their approaches were distinctive.

To be ready to situate these writers and their contributions in the context of others writing at the time, their antecedents, and those who followed after them.

course_details.Overview of class: This course explores the moral thought of one of the most influential figures in philosophy. Immanuel Kant systematizes and defends several familiar moral ideas, such as the unconditional authority of moral requirements and the dignity of each individual. He argues that acting morally is both a requirement of reason and the condition for our freedom, so that morally wrong action is both irrational and a kind of bondage. His approach to moral theory persists in its power, and remains one of a handful of live options among moral philosophers working today. We will engage in a careful study of this system, focusing on the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, and also reading parts of the Critique of Practical Reason, the Metaphysics of Morals, and Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason.
course_details.Registration Requirements: At least one prior writing-based philosophy class.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students will be expected to have an understanding of the basic concepts of Kant's moral theory and the relations among them, as well as knowledge of what makes a Kantian approach to moral theory distinctive.
course_details.Teaching Method: The course will be organized around lectures, with plenty of time for questions and discussion.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Argument reconstructions, papers, and in class final exam.

course_details.Overview of class: This course aims to uncover common throughlines in 20th century philosophy of language in both the Anglo-American and Continental philosophical traditions. We will read Wittgenstein, Austin, Gadamer, and Habermas to see what animates their thinking, and to put their ideas into conversation with each other. Special attention will be paid to understanding their views on the social nature of linguistic interpretation, and communicative action. This seminar will be oriented around entire books by the respective authors, and students will be assessed both on their written work and their detailed notes of the texts.

course_details.Overview of class: Should the study of society be value-free, and is that even possible? Starting from Max Weber's famous defense of Wertfreiheit (value freedom), this course examines debates about the fact/value distinction throughout the Twentieth Century, including readings drawn from natural right theory (Strauss), critical theory (Adorno and Habermas), hermeneutics (Taylor), pragmatism (Putnam), and feminist philosophy of science (Longino and Anderson).
course_details.Learning Objectives: Understand the best arguments for and against the idea of value-free social science.

course_details.Overview of class: The question What should I believe? is typically raised as an epistemological question, but many authors allow that it has a practical dimension as well. In this seminar we will explore two recent systematic attempts to address the question. These are found in Mona Simion's Resistance to Evidence (Cambridge University Press, 2024), and Matt McGrath's What Should We Believe? An Essay on Epistemic Normativity (Oxford University Press, forthcoming). These are the required books (both of which will be provided for free). We will address their books with an eye on addressing several subsidiary questions. First, what kind of question(s) can be asked with this language? What do these questions tell us about epistemic assessment? about epistemic normativity? What significance do these questions have for epistemology more generally?
course_details.Learning Objectives: The successful student (1) will be able to characterize the nature of the question(s) we are asking when we ask what we should believe, (2) will be able to identify how these questions bear on epistemic assessment, epistemic normativity, and epistemology more generally, and (3) will be able to express and defend an opinion on these matters in writing.
course_details.Evaluation Method:
The final grade will be a function of the class participation grade (20%) and the final paper grade (80%).

Students will be expected to come to class prepared to discuss the day's readings; students will be expected to run a class discussion at least once; and students will be expected to write a term paper at the end of the quarter.
